newsitem.title: INDIA: India coalition seen bruised, but not in peril.
newsitem.headline: India coalition seen bruised, but not in peril.

text.p: A regional party's threat to quit the government would not destabilise India's ruling coalition as long as it remained buttressed by the Congress party, analysts said on Tuesday.

Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's United Front coalition was jolted on Monday when the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) party said it planned to withdraw its four ministers but continue parliamentary support

Industry Minister Murasoli Maran's DMK party cited differences over the conduct of some unidentified coalition partners for its action, which follows a split on July 5 in Gujral's Janata Dal (JD) party. Janata Dal's then leader Laloo Prasad Yadav formed a breakaway Rashtriya Janata Dal (RJD) but stayed on in the 15-party alliance.

"Obviously it (the DMK action) has further hurt the credibility of the United Front (UF) government for effective governance," analyst Pran Chopra of the Centre for Policy Research (CPR) told Reuters.
"But it has not placed in peril the survival of the UF government any more than the split in the JD did so."
The centre-left United Front, which has 178 deputies in the 545-member lower house of parliament, was formed after elections last year with support from the Congress party's 140 members.
Congress' support aimed to keep from power the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), which controls 193 votes.

"As always, the UF's destiny does not lie in its own hands, but in those of its main prop. The Congress and its assessment of its own chances of coming to power will put its stamp on Indian policies," the Indian Express newspaper said in a commentary on Tuesday.

In numbers, the DMK has less than a tenth of the UF's total, but its statement on Monday rattled the coalition, formed last year with a "common minimum programme" to sink differences among regional parties, free market proponents and communists.
The DMK's president, Muthuvel Karunanidhi, said in the statement that the coalition had compromised its dignity.
"It (the statement) is more of a warning that he might contemplate pulling out," Chopra said.

DMK leaders said its warning was directed at the Communist Party of India-Marxist (CPI-M), which wanted Yadav to resign as chief minister of his eastern state of Bihar because he was indicted in a corruption scandal.
If Yadav did not go, his breakaway RJD group should be kicked out of the alliance, the CPI-M said.
Prime Minister Gujral wants Yadav to resign and face trial in the scandal, but he has refused to heed demands to sack three of Yadav's loyalist ministers in the federal government.
Yadav, who says he is innocent, assured support to Gujral but embarrassed the government by refusing calls to quit.
In a week of attacks on the coalition, the CPI-M has taken the lead in seeking the exit of Yadav in the $280-million scandal involving the alleged siphoning off of animal welfare funds.
Yadav had broken away from the party on July 5, citing alleged rigging of voting against him in the party's presidential elections held two days before.

The CPI-M says Yadav must go in the interests of a credible fight against corruption. But its general secretary, Harkishan Singh Surjeet, said on Monday that the crisis would blow over next week when he met the DMK's Karunanidhi.
But the squabble hurt the coalition's image.

"It doesn't require great political acumen to observe that dignity and adherence to principle were not among the UF's strong points right from the heady days when political expediency gave birth to the hydra-headed formation," the Indian Express said.
